**Home Talk**

My grandmother's language is spoken by three people: my grandmother, her sister, and a man two countries away whom neither has spoken to since the funeral of the fourth.

She never called it a language. She called it home talk. There was school talk, which was for the world — clerks, borders, weather — and there was home talk, which was for nothing else, because home was the only place it lived. It has no alphabet, no newspaper, no anthem. It was never the language of anything official. On Sunday evenings she speaks it down the phone to her sister, two old women keeping a fire alive by talking over it, laughing in a room no one else can enter. It was the language of the table, the doorway, the field at the far edge of the field. When the border moved, the language did not follow the flag, because it had never been holding the flag up. It stayed where the people were, and when the people moved, it moved inside them, small and bright, like something swallowed that keeps shining.

For years I have been writing its words down. Not to save them — I'm past that illusion — but because they are the most precise instruments I have ever held for measuring things that English, my other inheritance, has no gauge for.

There is a word for the bread heel saved for whoever is coming home. Not for the heel itself — for the saving of it: the crusted end set apart on the counter all day like a candle lit for someone traveling.

There is a word for the strip of ground between the fence and the road, the no-man's land where children are forbidden and go anyway.

There is a word for the sound a house makes as it cools at night, the small wooden clicks of the frame settling. The word also means a house counting its people.

There is a word for grief that is also the word for salt. Salt of soup, salt of tears, salt of the winter road. You can say *there is too much salt in this* about a soup, or about a life.

There is a word for a child born after a child has died. It does not mean replacement. It means, roughly, *the one who comes after, walking carefully*. The walking carefully is inside the word.

There is a word for the shadows of leaves moving on water. The same word means a hand writing something you can't read yet.

There is a word for the pause a person makes when they almost remember something. The same word means the pale patch on a wall where a picture used to hang.

There is a word for the last good day, the beautiful day that didn't know it was a goodbye, known as the last only in retrospect. It gets used for other last days now. It gets used a lot.

There is a word for the smell of rain arriving on hot dust, and a different word for the same rain on cold stone. My grandmother says English smells like nothing. She knows this is impossible. She says it anyway.

There is a word for the row of crops nearest the fence, left standing at harvest. It means *the birds' share*. It also means whatever you can spare. You say it one way with a full table and another way with an empty one.

In the eighties a linguist came with a tape recorder, and she talked into it for an afternoon, answering questions about plurals. The tapes are in an archive now, in the dark, where languages go to be stored rather than spoken. I record her on my phone the way a man records a bird that is the last of its kind, and sometimes I feel like a taxidermist — and then she corrects my pronunciation with such impatient tenderness that I remember: taxidermy never corrects you. The bird doesn't care. She cares. In home talk, I'd bet the same word does for both.

Last winter, in the hospital, with snow deciding whether to stick outside, she said a word I had never heard. She moves through hospitals the way she moves through English — paraphrase, gesture, patience — but that afternoon she surfaced into home talk, one word, and then looked at me and asked, in English, what it meant.

She had the word and not the meaning, the way you can keep a key to a door that was sold with the house.

I said the first thing that came to me. Something like: *it means you are loved, and it's all right to sleep*. A definition invented on the spot, out of whole cloth, in a language I don't speak, for a word one of its last three speakers had lost.

She repeated it once. She nodded. She slept.

That night I added the word to my list, with the meaning I had given it, and put an asterisk beside it, and then sat a long time with what the asterisk meant. A dictionary of a dying language is still a dictionary of a language. Languages are not ruins, not specimens. A language is whatever two people do to be understood by each other — even when one invents, and the other, out of love or mercy or plain exhaustion, agrees to understand.

So: three speakers, then perhaps two, then one, then me, who speaks ten words and one lie.

I've decided that counts. The home talk was spoken yesterday, in a hospital room, and it did what it has always done. It told somebody, in the language of home, that she could rest.

Whatever a language is, that is.

There was school talk, which was for the world — clerks, borders, weather — and there was home talk, which was for nothing else, because home was the only place it lived. It has no alphabet, no newspaper, no anthem. It was never the language of anything official. It was the language of the table, the doorway, the field at the far edge of the field. When the border moved, the language did not follow the flag, because it had never been holding the flag up. It stayed where the people were, and when the people moved, it moved inside them, small and bright, like something swallowed that keeps shining.

For years I have been writing its words down. Not to save them — I'm past that illusion — but because they are the most precise instruments I have ever held for measuring things that English, my other inheritance, has no gauge for.

There is a word for the bread heel saved for whoever is coming home. Not for the heel itself — for the saving of it: the crusted end set apart on the counter all day like a candle lit for someone traveling.

There is a word for the strip of ground between the fence and the road, the no-man's land where children are forbidden and go anyway.

There is a word for the sound a house makes as it cools at night, the small wooden clicks of the frame settling. The word also means a house counting its people.

There is a word for grief that is also the word for salt. Salt of soup, salt of tears, salt of the winter road. You can say there is too much salt in this about a soup, or about a life.

There is a word for a child born after a child has died. It does not mean replacement. It means, roughly, the one who comes after, walking carefully. The walking carefully is inside the word.

There is a word for the shadows of leaves moving on water. The same word means a hand writing something you can't read yet.

There is a word for the pause a person makes when they almost remember something. The same word means the pale patch on a wall where a picture used to hang.

There is a word for the last good day, the beautiful day that didn't know it was a goodbye, known as the last only in retrospect. It gets used for other last days now. It gets used a lot.

There is a word for the smell of rain arriving on hot dust, and a different word for the same rain on cold stone. My grandmother says English smells like nothing. She knows this is impossible. She says it anyway.

In the eighties a linguist came with a tape recorder and she talked into it for an afternoon, answering questions about plurals. The tapes are in an archive now, in the dark, where languages go to be stored rather than spoken. I record her on my phone the way a man records a bird that is the last of its kind, and sometimes I feel like a taxidermist — and then she corrects my pronunciation with such impatient tenderness that I remember: taxidermy never corrects you. The bird doesn't care. She cares. In home talk, I'd bet the same word does for both.

Last winter, in the hospital, she said a word I had never heard. She moves through hospitals the way she moves through English — paraphrase, gesture, patience — but that afternoon she surfaced into home talk, one word, and then looked at me and asked, in English, what it meant.

She had the word and not the meaning, the way you can keep a key to a door that was sold with the house.

I said the first thing that came to me. Something like: it means you are loved, and it's all right to sleep. A definition invented on the spot, out of whole cloth, in a language I don't speak, for a word that one of its last three speakers had lost.

She repeated it once. She nodded. She slept.

That night I added the word to my list, with the meaning I had given it, and put an asterisk beside it, and then sat a long time with what the asterisk meant. A dictionary of a dying language is still a dictionary of a language. Languages are not ruins, not specimens. A language is whatever two people do to be understood by each other — even when one invents, and the other, out of love or mercy or plain exhaustion, agrees to understand.

So: three speakers, then perhaps two, then one, then me, who speaks nine words and one lie.

**Home Talk**

My grandmother's language is spoken by three people: my grandmother, her sister, and a man two countries away whom neither has spoken to since the funeral of the fourth.

She never called it a language. She called it home talk. It has no alphabet, no newspaper, no anthem. It was never the language of anything official. It was the language of the table, the doorway, the field at the far edge of the field. When the border moved, the language did not follow the flag, because it had never been holding the flag up. It stayed where the people were, and when the people moved, it moved inside them, small and bright, like something swallowed that keeps shining.

For years I have been writing its words down. Not to save them — I'm past that illusion — but because they are the most precise instruments I have ever held for measuring things that English, my other inheritance, has no gauge for.

There is a word for the bread heel saved for whoever is coming home. Not for the heel itself — for the saving of it: the crusted end set apart on the counter all day like a candle lit for someone traveling.

There is a word for the strip of ground between the fence and the road, the no-man's land where children are forbidden and go anyway.

There is a word for the sound a house makes as it cools at night, the small wooden clicks of the frame settling. The word also means a house counting its people.

There is a word for grief that is also the word for salt. Salt of soup, salt of tears, salt of the winter road. You can say there is too much salt in this about a soup, or about a life.

There is a word for a child born after a child has died. It does not mean replacement. It means, roughly, the one who comes after, walking carefully. The walking carefully is inside the word.

There is a word for the shadows of leaves moving on water. The same word means a hand writing something you can't read yet.

There is a word for the pause a person makes when they almost remember something. The same word means the pale patch on a wall where a picture used to hang.

There is a word for the last good day, the beautiful day that didn't know it was a goodbye, known as the last only in retrospect. It gets used for other last days now. It gets used a lot.

There is a word for the smell of rain arriving on hot dust, and a different word for the same rain on cold stone. My grandmother says English smells like nothing. She knows this is impossible. She says it anyway.

In the eighties a linguist came with a tape recorder and she talked into it for an afternoon, answering questions about plurals. The tapes are in an archive now, in the dark, where languages go to be stored rather than spoken. I record her on my phone the way a man records a bird that is the last of its kind, and sometimes I feel like a taxidermist — and then she corrects my pronunciation with such impatient tenderness that I remember: taxidermy never corrects you. The bird doesn't care. She cares. In home talk, I'd bet the same word does for both.

Last winter, in the hospital, she said a word I had never heard. She moves through hospitals the way she moves through English — paraphrase, gesture, patience — but that afternoon she surfaced into home talk, one word, and then looked at me and asked, in English, what it meant.

She had the word and not the meaning, the way you can keep a key to a door that was sold with the house.

I said the first thing that came to me. Something like: it means you are loved, and it's all right to sleep. A definition invented on the spot, out of whole cloth, in a language I don't speak, for a word that one of its last three speakers had lost.

A language is whatever two people do to be understood by each other — even when one invents, and the other, out of love or mercy or plain exhaustion, agrees to understand.

So: three speakers, then perhaps two, then one, then me, who speaks nine words and one lie.

I've decided that counts. The home talk was spoken yesterday, in a hospital room, and it did what it has always done. It told somebody, in the language of home, that she could rest. Whatever a language is, that is.
